flags.note: 'hardly ______' with an un- word creates a double negative; tests careful reading but is legitimate. All four options share the un- prefix, so there is no length or form cue.

S047-01.notes: After the colon the passage says she admired one thing but mostly found fault, so her praise was held back: 'hardly unreserved'. A: nothing in the passage says she lacked knowledge. B: whether anyone asked for the review is irrelevant. D: the passage says nothing about originality. Inserted sentence: 'The critic's verdict on the new film was hardly unreserved: although...' reads cleanly.

flags.note: 'just as low' has no stated baseline because there is no pot without marigolds. The comparison between sterilized and unsterilized pots still supports A on its own.

S047-02.notes: Sterilizing the soil killed the fungi, yet the nematode reduction stayed the same, so the effect does not depend on fungi. B: the study did not compare fungi near marigolds with fungi near tomatoes. C: the study gives no information on harm to tomatoes. D: every pot had a marigold, so this cannot be inferred.

flags.note: The key is the only option that computes differences, and it is slightly the longest. The cue is mild. Its arithmetic is correct: 14-6=8 and 9-5=4.

S047-03.notes: The conclusion is that the app helped the below-grade group more, which needs a comparison of the advantage over nonusers in both groups. A: uses raw gains, which can't separate the app's effect from the group's baseline. B: covers only the at-grade group. C: shows the app helped both groups but not that it helped one group more.

S047-04.notes: Vint held television viewing roughly constant and still found differences in dialect use, so television is unlikely to be the cause. A: contradicts her 'not broadcast speech' claim. C: she never questions that the change happened. D: no text suggests television preserves dialect.

flags.note: Distractor A is noticeably the longest option, which works against the key rather than pointing to it. No other defects.

S047-05.notes: Putting the slip in the drawer of letters she 'did not intend to answer' implies she won't follow through on her promise. A: nothing in the text mentions finances or suppliers. B: she wrote the title down and studied it, so she has not forgotten it. D: the drawer suggests the opposite of writing to him.

S047-06.notes: Rail towns adopted standard time years before towns without rail service, which links the switch to railroads. A: shows railroads kept schedules, not that they ended sun time. C: points to a different factor. D: population growth is irrelevant to timekeeping. The historical premise, railroad standard time in 1883, is accurate.

S047-07.notes: The appositive opens with a dash, so it must close with one: '...a baker, and a local historian—never expected it...'. A: comma closes a dash-opened appositive (mismatched). B: semicolon leaves 'The festival's founders—...historian' as a fragment. C: leaves the appositive unclosed, so 'a local historian never expected' wrongly reads as its own clause. The meaning ('never expected... yet attracted 20,000') is logical.

S047-08.notes: The subject 'notebooks' needs a finite plural verb, so 'contain' is correct. B, C and D (containing / which contain / having contained) each leave the sentence without a main verb, so the result is a fragment. The long interrupter between subject and verb is the intended difficulty.

flags.note: 'wrongly as it turned out' may lure some takers to 'Nevertheless'. The logic still clearly supports cause and effect. The history is accurate: Newton's 1668 reflector came from his belief that chromatic aberration couldn't be corrected, and achromatic lenses came later.

S047-09.notes: Believing lenses couldn't be fixed, he built a mirror telescope, so the second step follows from the first: 'Accordingly'. B: the step is not a contrast with his conclusion. C: the sentence is not an example. D: no contrast is set up.

S047-10.notes: C is the only choice that gives the finding (4 vs 11) and also names a limitation (sulfur dioxide unmeasured, so other factors are possible). A: overclaims a cause and names no limitation. B: gives neither the finding nor a limitation. D: gives the limitation but not the finding.
